valuation.quote_listing: Euronext Amsterdam (AMS) — primary listing of Prosus N.V.

bull_thesis: Prosus is a consumer-internet holding company that you can buy for roughly two-thirds of what its assets are worth. At about 39.5 euros the shares trade at close to a 35% discount to net asset value (the market value of everything Prosus owns, minus debt). The single biggest thing it owns is a ~22.8% stake in Tencent, the Chinese internet giant — worth on its own around 121 billion dollars on Prosus's latest published tally, or roughly 76% of gross assets, which is more than Prosus's entire ~84 billion euro market value. In other words, you get the Tencent stake at a discount and the rest of the empire — Brazil's iFood (food delivery), OLX (classifieds), PayU (payments), eMAG, the newly-bought Just Eat Takeaway, plus listed stubs in Meituan, Delivery Hero, Trip.com and Swiggy — thrown in for less than nothing. Three things are actively shrinking that discount. First, the open-ended buyback: since 2022 the company has repurchased more than 40 billion dollars of its own stock, and because it buys below net asset value, every euro spent lifts net asset value per share for the holders who stay — management says the program has already added roughly 16 percentage points to net asset value per share. Second, the operating turnaround is real and delivered: the e-commerce businesses reached profitability for the first time ever, ahead of schedule, and CEO Fabricio Bloisi has hit his own targets (he promised 400 million dollars of e-commerce profit and delivered 443 million; ecosystem profitability jumped ~84% to about 1.3 billion dollars in fiscal 2026, with record free cash flow of ~1.5 billion). Third, capital allocation is rotating: Prosus is funding buybacks increasingly by selling smaller non-Tencent holdings (more than 2 billion dollars a year, with 'a few more billions' flagged for next year) rather than selling down its highest-conviction Tencent position. Entry timing is attractive — the stock sits only ~2% off its 52-week low and Tencent itself is depressed (about a third below its 52-week high), so you are buying a discounted claim on an already-marked-down anchor. If the discount narrows toward the high teens or low twenties (Morgan Stanley recently upgraded to overweight seeing ~29% upside on the view the discount has peaked) and Tencent recovers, both levers pull the same way.
bear_thesis: The reason Prosus is cheap is the reason it may stay cheap: it is a complex holding company whose value is dominated by a single, hard-to-control asset in a jurisdiction the market distrusts. Roughly 76% of gross asset value is one Chinese stock, Tencent, and Prosus holders own only a paper claim on it through a Dutch corporate wrapper — no direct shares, no ability to force a distribution. Tencent has already fallen from a 52-week high near HKD 683 to about HKD 460 (below its 200-day average), and China regulatory, macro and AI-competition fears could take it lower toward its 52-week low near 411; because Tencent is the bulk of net asset value, a further leg down in Tencent drops Prosus's fair value regardless of anything management does. The holding-company discount has proven stubborn for years and has narrowed only to ~35% — there is no contractual mechanism (no tender, no wind-up, no fixed payout) that forces it to close, and management itself concedes 'it was not built overnight… it will not disappear overnight.' Capital allocation is the live worry: rather than simply returning the cash pile, Prosus spent roughly 4.1 billion euros to take over Just Eat Takeaway, an asset the CEO himself calls 'not growing' and 'not performing well,' and the once-large net-cash cushion (about 4.4 billion dollars net cash a year ago) has swung to a modest net-debt position after that deal and continued buybacks. The buyback — the main engine of the thesis — is decelerating (guided to ~6-7 billion dollars a year versus ~7 billion prior), and the discount actually widened after the interim results when management signaled that deceleration. EdTech was a value-destroying 2021-vintage mistake, classifieds (OLX) face a genuine, if manageable, GenAI channel-shift risk (peers like Rightmove issued AI profit warnings), and the promotional 'execution, execution, execution / build 100 billion dollars outside Tencent' tone invites skepticism. Without a hard catalyst, this can remain a perpetual 'cheap for a reason' holdco.
sop_fair_value: ≈ 46 euros per share (base case), versus about 60 euros of estimated net asset value per share at today's marks — i.e. fair value applies a still-meaningful ~25% holding-company discount rather than assuming the discount fully closes.
sop_breakdown: Valuation is a sum-of-the-parts / net-asset-value exercise, since Prosus is a holding company. At today's marks estimated gross net asset value is roughly 60 euros per share: the Tencent stake (~22.8%, ~121 billion dollars) is by far the largest piece at roughly 50 euros per share and alone exceeds the ~39.5 euro share price; the unlisted e-commerce ecosystem (iFood, OLX, PayU, eMAG, Just Eat Takeaway, La Centrale, Despegar) contributes on the order of 18-22 euros per share on Prosus's private marks; other listed stubs (Meituan, Delivery Hero, Trip.com, Swiggy) add a few euros; less modest net debt (~5 billion dollars after the Just Eat deal and buybacks) and holding-company costs, roughly 2-3 euros per share. Base-case fair value of ~46 euros holds the discount at ~25% (versus ~35% today), and credits ongoing buyback accretion and e-commerce profit growth over the horizon with Tencent roughly flat. The bull case (~54 euros) assumes the discount narrows toward the high teens/low twenties and/or Tencent recovers off depressed levels. The bear case (~33 euros, below the current 52-week low) assumes Tencent legs down toward its 52-week low and the discount re-widens toward 40% on buyback deceleration and Just Eat integration disappointment.
risk_reward: Skewed favorably but slow-burn. From about 39.5 euros, the adverse case sees roughly 33 euros if Tencent — three-quarters of the asset base — falls further and the holding-company discount re-widens, taking the shares below their current 52-week low. The base case of about 46 euros requires only that the discount grind modestly tighter while the buyback keeps lifting net asset value per share, and the favorable case of about 54 euros needs the discount to compress toward the high teens and/or a Tencent recovery. The upside is larger than the downside, and entry near 52-week lows on an already-depressed Tencent improves the odds — but there is no hard event that forces the gap to close, so the payoff is a multi-quarter grind rather than a dated re-rating, and it carries live China/Tencent beta in the meantime.
peer_comps_note: The right comparison frame is not a price-to-earnings or price-to-free-cash-flow multiple (the screener's 49.7x price-to-free-cash-flow and 200% net margin are artifacts of periodic stake sales, not operating economics) but the discount to net asset value versus other holding companies — the peer set of Naspers (the South African parent, which trades at its own discount), and the underlying assets benchmarked against Tencent, MercadoLibre, Sea Ltd and Grab. Prosus's discount has narrowed from a historical 40-50% to about 35% today; Tencent is ~76% of gross asset value and is currently marked around 121 billion dollars, itself down about a third from its 52-week high. Morgan Stanley recently moved to overweight arguing the discount has peaked, seeing roughly 29% upside. The persistence of the discount is explained by China regulatory overhang, holding-company complexity/illiquidity, the Naspers cross-ownership structure, and capital-allocation uncertainty.
forcing_function: There is no single dated event that forces a re-rating — this is the catalyst's weakness. The re-rating pressure instead accumulates from repeated, self-reinforcing steps: the open-ended buyback executed below net asset value (each tranche lifts net asset value per share), programmatic sales of smaller non-Tencent holdings that fund it (more than 2 billion dollars this year, with management flagging 'a few more billions' next year and a likely announcement of the next year's disposal target within about six months), and the e-commerce profit ramp toward 'a couple of billion dollars of profit,' each visible at the semi-annual results (interim results around December, full-year around June). Harder potential catalysts that would shatter consensus faster would be a large asset disposal or IPO, or an activist pressing on the structure; absent those, the buyback-plus-disposals grind is the forcing function.
moderator_conclusion: Prosus is a genuinely cheap, improving holding company without a hard, dated catalyst — so the disciplined call is to wait for (or accept) weakness rather than chase, even though the entry point here is already attractive. What you are buying at about 39.5 euros on the Amsterdam listing is a claim, at roughly a 35% discount, on a portfolio that is ~76% one Chinese stock (Tencent) plus a now-profitable e-commerce ecosystem you effectively get for free. The value case is strong and stands on its own: net asset value per share is on the order of 60 euros at today's depressed Tencent mark, base-case fair value is about 46 euros holding a still-conservative ~25% discount, and the buyback mechanically compounds net asset value per share because the company is repurchasing below intrinsic value. Management's credibility has improved — they reached e-commerce profitability ahead of schedule, hit their own profit targets, and are rotating capital sensibly by funding buybacks with non-core disposals rather than selling their best asset. But the load-bearing driver — the discount narrowing — is a soft, non-binding catalyst that has been running for years with no contractual payout and no fixed date; management openly says it 'will not disappear overnight,' and the discount even widened after the last results when the buyback pace was trimmed. Two real risks temper conviction: Tencent is ~76% of the value and carries live China/AI/regulatory beta that can drop fair value irrespective of management action, and the ~4.1 billion euro Just Eat Takeaway purchase of an admittedly 'not growing' asset — which helped swing the balance sheet from net cash to modest net debt — is a capital-allocation question mark that helps explain why the discount persists. Net: wait-and-accumulate rather than aggressive entry. Real, self-funding value; a favorable but un-dated skew; hold-level conviction on the catalyst, a notch higher on the underlying value.
